Noble Eightfold Path: Buddhist practices leading to liberation from saṃsāra.
In Christian theology, this condition inherited from Adam and Eve's expulsion from Eden was shaped significantly by Augustine of Hippo — what is it called?
Original sin: Christian doctrine about human nature.
An economist who began as a Madrid city councillor in 2004, he's led Spain's Socialist Workers' Party and, since 2022, presided over Socialist International — which prime minister is it?
Pedro Sánchez: Prime Minister of Spain since 2018. Sánchez began his political career in August 2004 as a city councillor in Madrid, before being elected to the Congress of Deputies in 2009.

Head of the Catholic Church for nearly 32 years — the longest verified reign in history — this pontiff convened a council that defined papal infallibility before declaring himself a 'prisoner' after Rome's capture in 1870 — who was he?
Pope Pius IX: Head of the Catholic Church from 1846 to 1878.
This ideology holds that humans split into groups ranked as inherently superior or inferior, based on supposedly inherited and shared traits — what is it called?
Declared independent on a man-made platform in the Adriatic in 1968, this micronation used Esperanto as its official language before being demolished by Italian authorities — what was it called?
Republic of Rose Island: 1968 micronation in the Adriatic Sea. The Italian government viewed it as a ploy by Rosa to raise money from tourists while avoiding national taxation.
Born in Tampico, Illinois, this future actor started as a sports broadcaster in Iowa in 1933 before moving to Hollywood and later serving as Screen Actors Guild president twice. Who was he?
Ronald Reagan: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989.
Taken as a Mughal hostage at age nine to enforce his father's treaty, this man later ruled from 1681 to 1689 as the second king of a major Indian empire — who is he?
Sambhaji: Chhatrapati of the Marathas from 1681 to 1689.
Once a commander of Alexander the Great's elite infantry, this Macedonian general later ruled Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia, and Iran, founding an empire that bore his name — who was he?
Seleucus I Nicator: Macedonian general, Diadochus, and founder of the Seleucid Empire.
Spanning Emperor Hirohito's reign from 1926 to 1989, this period saw Japan's wartime totalitarian turn, defeat in World War II, and a nearly seven-year American-led occupation — which era?
Shōwa era: Period of Japanese history (1926–1989)
Co-founder of the real estate firm Sansiri, this billionaire businessman served as Thailand's 30th prime minister until a court removed him in 2024 over a cabinet appointment — who is he?
Srettha Thavisin: Prime Minister of Thailand from 2023 to 2024.

Serving as Turkey's Interior Minister from 2016 to 2023 after the surprise resignation of his predecessor, this deputy chairman of the Justice and Development Party was known for accusing opposition figures of siding with terrorists — who is he?
One of the fifty Nereids and daughter of the sea god Nereus, this Greek sea nymph appears in the Trojan War cycle of myth — who is she?
A legendary tenth-year siege in Greek mythology, sparked when Paris took Helen from her husband—immortalized in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey—what's this ancient conflict?
Trojan War: Legendary war in Greek mythology. The Trojan War was a legendary conflict in Greek mythology that took place around the thirteenth century or early twelfth century BC.
Born to a murdered Arvernian aristocrat, this Gallic chieftain united the tribes of Gaul in a doomed revolt against Julius Caesar's legions — who was he?
This Kenyan activist founded the tree-planting Green Belt Movement and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Who was she?
Called the 'father of modern Liberia,' he was the country's longest-serving president, drawing foreign investment and pursuing national unification from 1944 until his death in 1971 — who is he?
William Tubman: President of Liberia from 1944 to 1971. William Vacanarat Shadrach Tubman (29 November 1895 – 23 July 1971) was a Liberian politician.
A labour lawyer and longtime Communist Party member, which Spanish politician founded the left-wing alliance Sumar and serves as Second Deputy Prime Minister?
Yolanda Díaz: Spanish politician and lawyer (born 1971)
Which of these four is the eldest?
William Smith (geologist) (born 1769) is the earliest of the four. Financially ruined, Smith spent time in debtors' prison.
Who among these was born first?
Jan Hus (born 1369) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Which of these is a chemist?
Elizabeth Rona is a chemist. Elizabeth Rona (20 March 1890 – 27 July 1981) was a Hungarian nuclear chemist, known for her work with radioactive isotopes.
What is the atomic number of Tennessine?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
What is the atomic number of Astatine?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
In what year was Bill Wyman born?
Bill Wyman: William George Wyman (né Perks; born 24 October 1936) is an English musician who was the bassist of the rock band the Rolling Stones from 1962 to 1993.
In what year was Ferdinand Porsche born?
Ferdinand Porsche (3 September 1875 – 30 January 1951) was an Austrian-German automotive engineer and founder of the Porsche AG.
In what year did Pythagoras die?
Pythagoras: Pythagoras of Samos (Ancient Greek: Πυθαγόρας; c. 570 – c. 495 BC) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.
In what year did Richard Feynman die?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Molybdenum discovered?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
In what year was Titanium discovered?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Mikoyan MiG-27: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. It is based on the Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23 fighter aircraft, but optimised for air-to-ground attack.
In which country is Dassault Rafale based?
Dassault Rafale: France. Dassault built a technology demonstrator that first flew in July 1986 as part of an eight-year flight-test programme, paving the way for approval of the project.
Who is credited with discovering Technetium?
Technetium: Emilio G. Segrè. Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
Who is credited with discovering Cell theory?
Who is credited with discovering Hydrazine?
Hydrazine: Hermann Emil Fischer. Hydrazine is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula N2H4.
Sharing the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for unifying the weak and electromagnetic forces, who became the first Muslim scientist to win a Nobel?
Abdus Salam (29 January 1926 - 21 November 1996) was a Pakistani theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate.

Born into a prominent Stockholm family, this fluent-in-six-languages inventor filed his first patent at 24 and went on to hold 355 in all, while owning the arms-and-engineering firm Bofors. Who was he?
Alfred Nobel (noh-BEL; 21 October 1833 - 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
Its scientific name translates roughly to 'fused lizard,' and it may be the largest of its armored kind at up to 8 tons — which dinosaur genus?
Ankylosaurus is a genus of armored dinosaur. It was named by Barnum Brown in 1908; it is monotypic, containing only A. magniventris.

Around 1920, when the energy source of stars was a complete mystery, which English astrophysicist boldly and correctly guessed it was the fusion of hydrogen into helium — and lent his name to a natural ceiling on a star's brightness?
Arthur Eddington (28 December 1882 - 22 November 1944) was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.
Coming on over about 48 hours, this temporary one-sided facial paralysis of unknown cause can droop an eyebrow, alter taste, and make sounds painfully loud — what is it?
Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.
The third-most-produced bomber in history, this American four-engine heavy bomber dominated the European Theater and dropped more bombs than any other plane in WWII — which aircraft is it?
Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress is an American four-engined heavy bomber aircraft that was developed in the mid-1930s for the United States Army Air Corps (USAAC).

Synthesized by the liver in response to inflammation, this ring-shaped blood molecule binds to the surface of dead or dying cells to activate the immune system's complement cascade. What is it commonly called?
C-reactive protein (CRP) is an annular (ring-shaped) pentameric protein found in blood plasma, whose circulating concentration rises in response to inflammation.
Portuguese explorers carried this tropical American tree to India in the 16th century; today Ivory Coast and India lead a 3.9-million-ton global harvest of its nut — what is it?
Cashew is the common name of a tropical evergreen tree Anacardium occidentale, in the family Anacardiaceae.
Born in 1847, this American wore three hats at once — psychologist, logician, and mathematician. Who was she?
Christine Ladd-Franklin (December 1, 1847 - March 5, 1930) was an American psychologist, logician, and mathematician.
This activity involves designing algorithms and writing code in high-level languages so a machine can follow step-by-step instructions to perform tasks. What is it?
Computer programming is the composition of sequences of instructions, called programs, that computers can follow to perform tasks.

This closed sac within the body has a distinct wall of cells that are structurally abnormal compared to surrounding tissue, and may contain air, fluid, or semi-solid material — unlike a pus-filled abscess, what is it called?
Cyst is a closed sac in the body, having a distinct envelope and division compared with the nearby tissue.
Bred around 1890 in Thuringia by a tax collector seeking a loyal protector, this German working-dog breed is known in North America by a slightly different two-word name — which breed?
Dobermann is a German breed of medium-large working dog of pinscher type.
Working with George de Hevesy, this Hungarian chemist theorized that diffusion speed depends on a nuclide's mass and became the world's go-to expert at preparing polonium — who was she?
Elizabeth Rona (20 March 1890 - 27 July 1981) was a Hungarian nuclear chemist, known for her work with radioactive isotopes.

Built by a consortium of Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo for four NATO nations, this twin-engine canard delta-wing fighter grew out of the 1983 Future European Fighter Aircraft programme — which jet?
Eurofighter Typhoon is a European multinational twin-engine, supersonic, canard delta wing, multirole fighter.
Part of the dog family yet famous for a pointed snout and a brush-like tail, the 'true' members of this group belong to the genus Vulpes — what creature is it?
Fox are small-to-medium-sized omnivorous mammals belonging to several genera of the family Canidae.
Caught from a tiny waterborne protist and common in travelers and children, it brings fatty, sticky diarrhea and abdominal pain a week or three after exposure — what is this parasitic illness?
Giardiasis is a parasitic disease caused by the protist enteropathogen Giardia duodenalis (also known as G. lamblia).
This North Atlantic member of the true cod family is a fisheries staple in northern Europe, often smoked into varieties like Finnan haddie and the Arbroath smokie — what is it?
Haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a saltwater ray-finned fish from the family Gadidae, the true cods.

This extinct human species from the Middle Pleistocene may represent the last common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans — or a completely separate lineage altogether — what species is it?
Homo heidelbergensis is a species of archaic human from the Middle Pleistocene of Europe and Africa, as well as potentially Asia depending on the taxonomic convention used.

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this 19th-century Hungarian doctor demonstrated that a simple hygiene practice could drastically cut deaths from childbed fever, decades before germ theory was widely accepted — who is he?

Ignaz Semmelweis (1 July 1818 - 13 August 1865) was a Hungarian medical doctor and scientist of German descent who was an early pioneer of antiseptic procedures and was described as the "saviour of mothers".
This 17th-century Dutch microscopist proved that an insect's egg, larva, pupa, and adult are all one creature, and in 1658 became the first to observe and describe red blood cells — who was he?
Jan Swammerdam (February 12, 1637 - February 17, 1680) was a Dutch biologist and microscopist.
A founder of modern geometric analysis, this American mathematician won the 2019 Abel Prize for pioneering work in geometric PDEs and gauge theory — who is she?
Karen Uhlenbeck (born August 24, 1942) is an American mathematician and one of the founders of modern geometric analysis.
This small Arctic rodent is a key prey source for tundra carnivores and is the subject of a persistent myth that it marches off cliffs in mass suicide — what animal is it?
Lemming is a small rodent, usually found in or near the Arctic in tundra biomes.
This evergreen tree, native to the cooler hills of south-central China, is grown commercially for its orange fruit and is sometimes called the Japanese medlar. What is it?
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
This computer scientist led the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer and is credited with coining the very term 'software engineering' — who is she?
Margaret Hamilton (software engineer) (ne Heafield; born August 17, 1936) is an American computer scientist.
This medication treats nausea, vomiting, and acid reflux by blocking dopamine receptors, but is rarely recommended for more than twelve weeks due to a risk of movement disorders — what drug is it?
Metoclopramide is a medication used to treat nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease.
This Bangladeshi economist pioneered microcredit and founded Grameen Bank, work that earned him the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before he later led an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus (born 28 June 1940) is a Bangladeshi economist and statesman.

Discovered in a fossil-rich West African formation and first described in 1976 but not formally named until 1999, this rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur lived roughly 115 to 105 million years ago — which genus?
Nigersaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived during the middle Cretaceous period, about 115 to 105 million years ago.
This flowering herb in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean, is sometimes called wild marjoram and is a staple of countless savory dishes. What is it?
Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
This New York Times columnist of 24 years was the sole winner of the 2008 Nobel in economics for explaining the patterns of international trade and where economic activity clusters. Who is he?
Paul Krugman (born February 28, 1953) is an American economist who is the Distinguished Professor of Economics at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York.

This branch of linguistics studies how languages organize their foundational sound units — like the contrast between 'bat' and 'gnat' — or, in sign languages, elements like hand shape and location — what is it called?
Phonology (formerly also phonemics or phonematics) is the branch of linguistics that concerns how languages organize the foundational elements that make their words.

Native to most of the Northern Hemisphere, this genus of 25 to 30 deciduous tree species includes poplars, aspens, and cottonwoods, one of which was the first tree ever fully DNA-sequenced — which genus?
Populus is a genus of 25-30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere.

Brought from China to Europe in the sixteenth century and popularized by the House of Orange in the Netherlands, this dog breed is known for its wrinkly, short-muzzled face and curled tail — name the breed?
Pug is a breed of dog with the physically distinctive features of a wrinkly, short-muzzled face, and curled tail.
This positive-sense RNA virus in the Enterovirus genus is the most common viral infectious agent in humans and the leading cause of the common cold — name the virus?
Rhinovirus (from the Ancient) is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Enterovirus in the family Picornaviridae.
This American painter turned inventor co-developed a telegraph system and became the namesake of the dot-dash code that helped make telegraphy commercially viable — who is he?
Samuel Morse (April 27, 1791 - April 2, 1872) was an American inventor and painter.
Before becoming the first woman on Facebook's board, this executive ran global sales at Google and assisted Lawrence Summers at the World Bank — who later wrote 'Lean In'?
Sheryl Sandberg (born August 28, 1969) is an American technology executive, philanthropist and writer.
This leafy green vegetable's high oxalate content gives raw and cooked versions noticeably different flavors, with blanching helping to tone it down — what vegetable is it?
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia.
These large waterfowl of the genus Cygnus are close relatives of geese and ducks, and are known for typically mating for life. What birds are they?
Swan are birds of the genus Cygnus within the family Anatidae.
Classed among the saurischians and placing them nearer to sauropodomorphs than to ornithischians, these hollow-boned, three-toed dinosaurs were ancestrally meat-eaters — which clade?
Theropoda (from ancient Greek -) is one of the three major clades of dinosaur, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha.
One of the earliest arthropod groups ever to appear in the fossil record, this extinct marine creature persisted in the oceans for nearly 270 million years across over 22,000 species — what is it?
Trilobite (meaning "three-lobed entities") are extinct marine arthropods that form the class Trilobita.
Its wild form is dioecious while domesticated versions bear hermaphrodite flowers — this Mediterranean-native plant is the ancestor of nearly all wine and table varieties — what species?

Vitis vinifera is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran.
Almost always found combined with lanthanide minerals and never on its own in nature, this element with symbol Y is a key ingredient in the phosphors used inside LEDs — which element?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.

The only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, this English mathematician saw that Charles Babbage's analytical engine could do far more than crunch numbers — earning her a reputation as the first computer programmer. Who was she?
Shining as the brightest star in Taurus some 67 light-years from Earth, this red giant has swollen to roughly 45 times the Sun's size despite a cooler surface — which star?
Aldebaran: Taurus Brightest Star. Aldebaran (Arabic: الدَّبَرَان, lit. 'The Follower') is a star in the zodiac constellation of Taurus.
Used to treat dangerous heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, which drug can take weeks to work when swallowed but carries risks of lung, liver, thyroid, and eye toxicity?

Serving as Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures while secretly working as the 'fourth man' of a notorious spy ring, this British art historian wrote a landmark 1967 study of the painter Nicolas Poussin — who is he?
Anthony Blunt: British art historian and Soviet spy (1907–1983)
Ranging from a racing tachycardia to a sluggish bradycardia, this catch-all term covers any heartbeat that strays from normal sinus rhythm — what is it called?
Arrhythmia: Group of medical conditions characterized by irregular heartbeat.
This Mexican mole salamander never grows up — it reaches sexual maturity while staying fully aquatic with feathery external gills, skipping metamorphosis entirely. What is it?
Axolotl: Species of salamander. The axolotl (from Classical Nahuatl: āxōlōtl [aːˈʃoːloːtɬ]; Ambystoma mexicanum) is a species of mole salamander.
A largely self-taught naturalist and astronomer born to a free mother in Maryland, he helped survey the District of Columbia and corresponded with Thomas Jefferson — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker: American scientist, surveyor and farmer (1731–1806)

In this distributed ledger, each record holds a cryptographic hash of the one before it, so altering a single block would require rewriting every block that follows — making the data nearly tamper-proof. What is it?
Blockchain: Distributed data store for digital transactions.

Originating from feral Eastern Mediterranean populations, this single wild plant species has been cultivated into an astonishing range of vegetables including broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts. What is it?
Brassica oleracea: Species of plant. Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.
The world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance works by mimicking adenosine's shape and blocking its receptors, keeping you awake — what is this stimulant?

This German-Swedish pharmacist had a knack for discovery — molybdenum, tungsten, barium, chlorine, and arguably oxygen all trace to his bench — but the same hands-on chemistry may have killed him via mercury poisoning. Which unlucky genius is it?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele: Swedish German chemist who discovered oxygen (1742–1786)
Descended from land mammals but now fully aquatic, this group swims via up-and-down tail strokes and includes toothed members capable of echolocation — what group includes whales and dolphins?
With about 3,400 species in over 520 genera, this insect family includes nearly every member of its group except two species in a small sister taxon — which family?
Native to tropical Africa and Asia, this plant genus produces caffeine-rich seeds that are roasted and brewed into one of the world's most valuable traded commodities — which genus?
This group of RNA viruses, named for the club-shaped spikes that crown their surface, causes illnesses ranging from the common cold to SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what are they called?
Coronavirus: Subfamily of viruses in the family Coronaviridae.
Named after the bladder because it was first found in urine, this amino acid carries a thiol group that lets it forge the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together. Which amino acid is it?
Cysteine: Proteinogenic amino acid. Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HS−CH2−CH(NH2)−COOH.
Native to South and Southeast Asia, this is the sole species in its genus and lives in large, non-hierarchical clans with several breeding females — what's this wild canid called?
Dhole: Species of mammal. The dhole ( dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.

With nearly 24,000 ommatidia in each compound eye and wings usually held flat rather than folded, this iridescent flying insect is often confused with its lighter-bodied damselfly cousins — what is it?
Appointed to the Supreme Court by Barack Obama in 2010, this former Harvard Law dean became the fourth woman ever to serve as a justice — who is she?
Elena Kagan: US Supreme Court justice since 2010.
A rod-shaped gut bacterium that's mostly harmless or even helpful — some strains produce vitamin K2 and fend off nastier microbes — what is its name?
Sold in Italian restaurants as branzino, this slow-growing ocean fish is the most important species farmed commercially in the Mediterranean — what fish is it?
European seabass: Species of fish. It is one of only six species in its family, Moronidae, collectively called the temperate basses.
Belonging to the genus Abies, these evergreen conifers have cones that stand upright like candles and disintegrate at maturity, and some varieties serve as Christmas trees — which conifer genus?
Fir: Genus of coniferous trees. The genus is most closely related to Keteleeria, a small genus confined to eastern Asia.
The largest region of the brain's cerebral hemispheres, this most-forward area contains the primary motor cortex and is separated from the parietal and temporal regions by two grooves — what is it?
Frontal lobe: Part of the brain. The most anterior ventral, orbital end of the frontal lobe is known as the frontal pole, which is one of the three so-called poles of the cerebrum.
First described by J. D. Hooker in 1889 and nicknamed the Transvaal or Barberton daisy for its South African origins, what genus of flowering plant is this?
Gerbera: Genus of plants. Gerbera ( JUR-bər-ə or GUR-bər-ə) L. is a genus of plants in the Asteraceae (Compositae) family.
This system of rules governing clauses, phrases, and word use is often absorbed unconsciously in childhood, long before anyone studies its syntax formally — what field?
Grammar: Structural rules of a language.

Marketed under a well-known brand name, this typical antipsychotic treats everything from schizophrenia to Tourette tics, but carries risks of tardive dyskinesia and dangerous QT-interval prolongation — what drug is it?
Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic medication. Haloperidol, sold under the brand name Haldol among others, is a typical antipsychotic medication.
Some called egrets and others bitterns, these 75 species of long-legged, long-beaked wading birds make up the family Ardeidae — what are they?
Heron: Family of birds. The OED also observes that shiterow or shederow are terms used for herons, and also applied as derogatory terms meaning a thin, weakly person.
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor. It is a simple pnictogen hydride, and is a colourless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odour.
The world's largest jet airliner when it first flew in 1963, this Soviet quad-engine jetliner entered Aeroflot service with a Moscow-to-Montreal flight in 1967. What aircraft?
Ilyushin Il-62: Soviet long-range narrow-body four-engined jet airliner.
An Indian polymath and pioneer of radio microwave optics, he's also considered the father of Bengali science fiction — and even has a crater on the Moon named for him. Who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose: Physicist, biologist and botanist (1857–1937)
On January 26, 1926, this Scottish inventor gave the world's first demonstration of a working mechanical television system — who is he?
Derived from Greek words for 'movement' and 'study,' this scientific field examines biomechanics, motor control, and rehabilitation to understand how the human body moves — what field is this?
Kinesiology: Study of human body movement. Kinesiology addresses physiological, anatomical, biomechanical, pathological, neuropsychological principles and mechanisms of movement.
Soft, dense, and bluish-silver when freshly cut, this heavy metal carries the highest atomic number of any stable element — and its Latin name, plumbum, gives it the symbol Pb. Which element is it?
Lead: Chemical element with atomic number 82 (Pb)
Understood before 1950 purely as the ability to decode written words, this concept later expanded to include the social and cultural dimensions of reading and writing — what skill is it?
Literacy: Ability to read and write.
Encoded by the codons AAA and AAG, this basic, essential amino acid cannot be synthesized by the human body — which one is it?
Lysine: Amino acid. Lysine (symbol Lys or K) is an α-amino acid that is a precursor to many proteins.

The first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win two, this Polish-born physicist and chemist discovered revolutionary elements and shared groundbreaking research on radioactivity with her husband—making her one of history's most influential scientists. Who was she?
Marie Curie: Polish-French physicist and chemist (1867–1934)
This waxy crystalline compound from peppermint and corn mint produces a cooling sensation when inhaled or rubbed on skin, and brings local-anesthetic relief to a sore throat — what is it?
Menthol: Organic compound used as flavouring and analgesic.
NATO nicknames it 'Foxhound,' and at roughly 3,000 km/h it's the fastest operational combat aircraft known — which interceptor, a Soviet successor to the MiG-25, is it?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Interceptor aircraft. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).

Synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and named in 2016 for the Russian region around it, this element 115 has a most-stable isotope lasting just 0.65 seconds — what is it?
Moscovium: Chemical element with atomic number 115 (Mc)

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena.
Made from red algae and dried into flat sheets through a process resembling papermaking, this ingredient has wrapped sushi and rice balls in Japan since the 700s — what is it?
Nori: Edible seaweed species of the red algae genus Pyropia.
Its Greek name means 'serpent-bearer,' and it's depicted as a man grasping a snake represented by a neighboring constellation — which constellation straddles the celestial equator?
Ophiuchus: Constellation straddling the celestial equator. Ophiuchus ( o-fee-YOO-kəs) is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator.
This butterfly was the first species to be given the common name now applied to its entire family, and is widespread across the Palearctic and North America — which species?
Papilio machaon: Species of insect. Papilio machaon, the Old World swallowtail, is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae.

This term for 'parts in each thousand' is symbolized by ‰ — a percent sign with an extra zero — and sits right next to the percent sign in Unicode's General Punctuation block — what is this unit called?
Per mille: Unit for parts per thousand. The associated symbol is ‰, similar to a per cent sign % but with an extra zero in the divisor.

Also known as physiography, this branch of natural science studies the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere — as opposed to the branch focused on the built human environment. Which field of study?
Physical geography: Study of processes and patterns in the natural environment.

Derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and capable of biodegrading, this thermoplastic polyester made up about a quarter of the world's bioplastic market in 2022 — what compound is this?
This deciduous member of the rose family includes many varieties known as plums in English, with greengages and damsons among its subspecies — which species is it?
Prunus domestica: Species of flowering plant.

Historically nicknamed 'hydrophobia' because sufferers panic at the offer of a drink, this viral disease causes severe brain inflammation and is virtually always fatal once symptoms appear. What is it?
Rabies: Deadly viral disease, transmitted through animals.
Responsible for at least half of all common colds, this tiny RNA virus in the Picornaviridae family measures only about 30 nanometers across — what is it?
Discovered in 1844 by Karl Ernst Claus and named in honor of Russia, which unreactive platinum-group element with atomic number 44 now caps extreme ultraviolet photomasks for chip lithography?
Ruthenium: Chemical element with atomic number 44 (Ru)
Exceeding 30 centimeters in length, this centipede from South America is the largest of its kind, preying on animals as large as small mammals and reptiles — which species?

Scolopendra gigantea: Species of Chilopoda (centipede). Scolopendra gigantea, also known as the Peruvian giant yellow-leg centipede or Amazonian giant centipede, is a centipede in the genus Scolopendra.

This medical condition of inadequate blood flow to body tissues comes in four flavors — hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive — and can progress to confusion or cardiac arrest if untreated — what is it called?
Shock (circulatory): Medical condition of insufficient blood flow. Shock is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.
